# Tūmatauenga: the stories first, then the spelling

The marks in **Tūmatauenga** make the most sense standing next to the myths they have to carry. So the myths come first.

## The Stories That Carry the Name

**The Sons of Ranginui and Papatūānuku.** In the beginning the Sky Father Ranginui and the Earth Mother Papatūānuku lay locked together in an embrace, and their children lived crushed in darkness between them.  Among the sons was Tūmatauenga, fiercest of them all.  When the brothers debated what to do, it was Tū who urged the final solution — kill the parents and have done.

**The One Who Stood.** Tāwhirimātea, god of winds and storms, had opposed the separation of his parents, and now he took war to his brothers in revenge, riding the weapon-winds of his storm-army.  Tangaroa fled to the sea; Tāne withdrew into the forests; Rongo and Haumia thrust themselves into the earth — but Tūmatauenga alone stood fast on the open plain, unbowed under the tempest (Grey, Polynesian Mythology).  When the storm at last spent itself, the standing one turned on his fleeing brothers and made their domains his own: he wove nets and took Tangaroa's fish, set snares for Tāne's birds, and dug into the earth for Rongo's kūmara and Haumia's fern-root.

**The Arts Won by Conquest.** By subduing his brothers, Tūmatauenga made their realms noa — common, usable — and so gave humankind its technologies: the net and hook for the sea, the snare for the forest, the digging-stick for the garden.  The karakia of planting, fishing, fowling, and war all carry his name, for every tapu those arts break was broken first by him; Best and Tregear record his invocation where food is made safe to eat.  The cycle thus makes the fiercest god the culture-bringer: not Tāne the gentle separator but Tū the stander, who gathered what the storm scattered and portioned it out.

## And Here Is What the Spelling Preserves

The restoration keeps one feature the ASCII form *tumatauenga* cannot show:

- **u → ū** — Macron marks the long vowel: how long the vowel is held.

A storyteller pronouncing the name would restore every one of them by instinct. The file only writes down what the voice already knows.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Tūmatauenga
- **ASCII form:** tumatauenga
- **Meaning:** "'The man of furious face' (tū + mata + ēngā), god of war and of humankind"
- **Domain of influence:** War, Humanity, Strength
- **Pantheon:** Polynesian
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** —
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 498 of 546

## The Name Travels

He is one face of a Polynesian-wide god: Hawaiian Kū — the great war-god of the heiau temples — Tahitian Tū, first ancestor as well as war-god, and the Cook Islands' war deities share his name and his office, the deepest layer of pan-Polynesian religion.  In New Zealand his worship ran through the war-parties and their tohunga; the nineteenth-century Māori military genius — the gunfighter pa of the New Zealand Wars — applied his standing to musket and trench, and the New Zealand Army today bears his name as its own: Ngāti Tūmatauenga, 'the tribe of the war-god.

## The Address It Earned

The temple of **Tūmatauenga** stands at [/tumatauenga/](/tumatauenga/) — [lore](/tumatauenga/lore/), [scholars](/tumatauenga/scholars/), [patterns](/tumatauenga/patterns/) — because a name carrying this much story deserves more than a parking page. The restoration preserves more than the ASCII form can express — stress, length, or a letter the Latin keyboard lost — which places it, mechanically, in Tier-1.
